```{r read in data, message = FALSE}
#data in Draft Rates by property 26.27 - statistical purposes 1 in two sheets. Data and Unit Rates

#===== Read in data ======#
Data <- read_excel("Draft Rates by property 26.27 - statistical purposes 1.xlsx", sheet = "Data", skip = 2) %>%
  drop_na(property_no) #first two rows are blank, Can map headers from unit_rates reference data set. Last rows are totals, but totals have no property number, so drop. 
# Unit_Rates <- read_excel("Draft Rates by property 26.27 - statistical purposes 1.xlsx", sheet = "Unit Rates")
wdc_rates <- read_csv("wdc_rates_qv.csv") %>% 
  mutate(rate_yr = factor(rate_yr, levels = c("22_23", "23_24", "24_25", "25_26", "26_27"), ordered = TRUE))

#CPI data for indexing
CPI <- read.csv("CPI.csv") %>%
  mutate(Date = as.Date(Date, format = "%d-%m-%Y"),
         year = year(Date)) %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(CPI = mean(CPI..Annual...change.))

#===== map setup begin ======#
nz <- read_sf("https://www.massey.ac.nz/~jcmarsha/data/nz_map/sa3_data.sqlite")

ta_nz <- nz %>% 
  group_by(territorial_authority, regional_council) %>%
  summarise(geometry = st_union(GEOMETRY), .groups = 'drop')

whanganui <- nz %>% filter(territorial_authority == "Whanganui District") %>%
  mutate(sa3_name = recode(sa3_name,
                           "Otamatea (Whanganui District)" = "Otamatea",
                           "Whanganui District Rural" = "Rural",
                           "Bastia-Durie Hill-Putiki" = "Bastia-Durie"))

bbox <- st_bbox(whanganui)

w_bbox <- list(x = c(1767500, 1779000), y=c(5574000, 5585000))
#===== map setup finish ======#

#===== Mapping Suburbs begin =====#
St_John_Streets <- c('Acton Pl', 'Aiken Rd', 'Alexa Pl', "Brassey Rd","Bristow St", "Chittick Pl","Collier Pl", "Dickson Cres", "Halswell St","Halswell Street","Hillside Tce", "Kent Rd","Linda Pl", "Ngapuhi St", "Oakland Ave","Parkes Ave", "Parsons St", "Porritt St", "Rawhiti Pl", "Smart Tce", "St Leonard St","Taranaki St","Tarata St", "Tregarth St","Tulloch St", "Virginia Rd", 'Peakes Rd', 'Victoria Park', 'Virginia Lake (Rotokawau)')

Otamatea_Streets <- c('Sewerage Pump Turere', 'Babbage Pl', 'Beachcroft', "Chelsea Cl", "Cotswolds Cl", "Diana Pl", "Eaton Cres", "Edith Collier Dr", "Edmonds Dr", "Goldsbury Pl", "Gumtree Rise", "Holdsworth Dr", "Kawau Pl", "Lancewood Pl", "Lithgow Dr", "Mannington Rd", "Montgomery Rd", "Norfolk Dr", "Otamatea Reserve", "Perrett Dr", "Pickwick Rd", "Rotokawau Dr", "Sandcroft Dr", "Sandy Lane", "St Johns Hts", "Suffolk Dr", "Tasman Views", "Tirimoana Pl", "Turere Pl","Virginia Hts", "Webster Pl", "Pukeko Drive", 'Tangaroa View', 'Middens Way')

Springvale_streets <-c('Addenbrooke Tce')

Whanganui_Centre_Streets <- c('Pitt St', 'Peat Pl', 'Peat St')

#===== Mapping suburbs finish =====

#===== Data wrangling begin =====
streets <- wdc_rates %>% 
  filter(suburb == "St Johns/Otamatea") %>% 
  select(property_no, rate_yr, property_address, suburb) %>%
  mutate(
    house_num = as.integer(str_extract(property_address, "^\\s*(\\d+)")), 
    street = str_remove(property_address, "~.*"),
    street = str_remove(street, "-."),
    street = str_remove(street, "^(?i:unit\\s+)?(?:[\\d/][\\d/A-Za-z]*\\s+)+"), #handles numbers and numbers like 9A,alos UNIT 6C / 59 and
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    suburb = case_when(
      #house numbers on great north road. great north road spans both. Lower number in St Johns up to 117. Then 119 and 121 are St Johns. 118, 120 and 122 onwards are otamtea
      street == "Great North Rd" & is.na(house_num) ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street == "Great North Rd" & house_num <= 117 ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street == "Great North Rd" & house_num %in% c(119, 121) ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street == "Great North Rd" & house_num >= 118 ~ "Otamatea (Whanganui District)",
      #easier ones
      street %in% St_John_Streets ~ "St Johns Hill",
      street %in% Otamatea_Streets ~ "Otamatea (Whanganui District)",
      street %in% Springvale_streets ~ "Springvale",
      street %in% Whanganui_Centre_Streets ~ "Whanganui Centre",
      TRUE ~ suburb
    )
  ) %>% select(property_no, rate_yr, suburb) #for left join

#join tdatasets to get what I need. Remove nulls from data set.
Rates <- wdc_rates %>% 
  filter(!is.na(assessment_number)) %>%
  left_join(
    Data %>% select(property_no, SUIP), 
    by = 'property_no') %>%
  mutate( #mapping qv_category to res/com/farm for simpler groupings
    Category = case_when(
      `qv category` %in% c('Commercial', 'Industrial') ~ 'Commercial', 
      `qv category` %in% c('Farming', 'Dairy', 'Pastoral', 'Forestry', 'Horticulture', 'Mining') ~ 'Farming',
      `qv category` %in% c('Other', 'Specialist', 'Utility asset') ~ 'Specialist',
      `qv category` %in% c('Residential', 'Lifestyle') ~ 'Residential',
      TRUE ~ `qv category`),
    SUIP = case_when(
      `qv category` == 'Mining' ~ 1,
      `qv category` == 'Residential' & is.na(SUIP) ~ 1,
      TRUE ~ SUIP)
    ) %>%
  left_join(streets, by = c('property_no', 'rate_yr'), suffix = c("", "_new")) %>%
  mutate(suburb = coalesce(suburb_new, suburb)) %>%
  mutate(
    suburb = recode(suburb,
    "Bastia/Durie Hills Putiki" = "Bastia-Durie Hill-Putiki",
    "Whanganui Central" = "Whanganui Centre",
    "Whanganui Rural" = "Whanganui District Rural",)
  ) %>%
  mutate(year = case_when(
    rate_yr == '22_23' ~ 2022,
    rate_yr == '23_24' ~ 2023,
    rate_yr == '24_25' ~ 2024,
    rate_yr == '25_26' ~ 2025,
    rate_yr == '26_27' ~ 2026,
    TRUE ~ NA,
    ),
    QV = cv + lv + (cv - lv),
    rate_per_m = `rate area (ha)` * 10000) %>%
  mutate(Category = factor(Category, 
                           levels = c('Specialist', 'Farming', 'Commercial', 'Residential'))) %>% #for consistent color coding
  select(-suburb_new) %>%
  mutate(suburb = recode(suburb, 
                         "Otamatea (Whanganui District)" = "Otamatea",
                         "Whanganui District Rural" = "Rural",
                         "Bastia-Durie Hill-Putiki" = "Bastia-Durie"))

#ranking for suburbs by median rates in 2026
Suburb_rank <- Rates %>%
  filter(Category == "Residential", year == 2026) %>%
  group_by(suburb) %>% 
  summarise(m = median(`total rates`)) %>%
  mutate(rank = rank(-m, ties.method = "min")) %>%   
  arrange(rank)    
  

Residential <- Rates %>%
  filter(Category == "Residential") %>%
  mutate(suburb = factor(suburb, levels = Suburb_rank$suburb))

#===== Data wrangling finish =====#

#===== Colour palette setup =====#
whanganui_palette <- function(n = 13, which = NULL) {
  pal <- c( #from inspecting the page elements of the Whanganui website, then color dropper picking from the coat of arms
  "#2757A2", 
  "#FEC30E",
  "#AD1619",
  "#008242", 
  "#DCC0E2", 
  "#C7E9F3",
  "#687928",
  "#D4582A",
  "#8B514E",
  "#93735B",
  "#372502",
  "#004925",
  "#FEEAD7",
  "black")
  
  if (!is.null(which)) {
    pal[which]
  }
  else if (n <= length(pal)) {
    pal[seq_len(n)]
  } else {
    grDevices::colorRampPalette(pal)(n)
  }
}

#===== Custom theme =====#
# font is Inter sans-serif, from website inspect elements on Whanganui council

theme_report <- function(base_size = 15) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "Inter") +
    theme(
      # Titles
      plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 18, hjust = 0,
                                   margin = margin(b = 5)),
      # Axes
      axis.title = element_text(size = 18),
      axis.text = element_text(size = 15),
      # Facet strips
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
      # Legend
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.title = element_text(size = 15),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 15),
      # Caption
      plot.caption = element_text(size =15)
    )
}

theme_map <- function(base_size = 15) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "Inter") +
    theme(
      # panels
      panel.grid.major = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      # Titles
      plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15, hjust = 0),
      # Axes
      axis.title =  element_blank(),
      axis.text =  element_blank(),
      # Legend
      legend.title = element_text(size = 15),
      legend.text = element_text(size = 15)
    )
}
```

# Graph 0: rates over time vs RBNZ inflation

In rate year 2025/26 Whanganui council had the lowest rates in the country. Across NZ, rates are typically consistently higher than the CPI inflation rate. This means that rate increases that outpace CPI are in effect, a tax. Relative to 2022 (when the data used starts) the year on year rate increase for Whanganui outpaced CPI, except in the years 2022/23 and 2026/27, with the 2025/26 year being only marginally higher than the annual average CPI (~5%).  
All this creates discussion around who pays the most rates and are people paying their 'fair share'. 

```{r graph 0, fig.width = 10, fig.height=4}
#RBNZ pink #ed1166
RBNZ_inflation <- CPI %>% filter(year >= 2022)
CPI_2022 <- RBNZ_inflation %>% filter(year == 2022) %>% pull(CPI)

#indexing rates to inflations, then getting % change ot compare next to CPI
timeseries_data <- Rates %>% #filter(Category == 'Residential') %>%
  arrange(property_no, year) %>%
  left_join(RBNZ_inflation, by = "year") %>%
  mutate(indexed_rates = (`total rates` / CPI) * CPI_2022) %>%
  group_by(property_no) %>%
  mutate(pct_change = (indexed_rates - lag(indexed_rates)) / lag(indexed_rates) * 100,
         pct_change = replace_na(pct_change, 0)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(property_no, year, `total rates`, indexed_rates, pct_change, Category)

G0_data <- timeseries_data %>%
  group_by(Category, year) %>%
  summarise(mean_pct_change = mean(pct_change), .groups = 'drop') 

CPI_rate <- G0_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = mean_pct_change, x = year, col = Category)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2,show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_line(data = RBNZ_inflation, aes(y = CPI, x = year, color = "RBNZ Inflation Rate"), linewidth = 1, linetype= 'dashed') +
  geom_point(data = RBNZ_inflation, aes(y = CPI, x = year, color = "RBNZ Inflation Rate"), size = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  #Scale arguments
  scale_x_continuous(labels = x_labels) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(round(min(G0_data$mean_pct_change),0), 
                                  round(max(G0_data$mean_pct_change),0)),
                      breaks = scales::breaks_width(20)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    setNames(whanganui_palette(4), c('Specialist', 'Farming', 'Commercial', 'Residential')),
    "RBNZ Inflation Rate" = "#ed1166"),
    name= "Legend") +
  #labels
  labs(title = 'Whanganui year on year mean rate percentage change against RBNZ CPI',
       subtitle = 'Rates changes are usually higher than CPI, except for 2026/27',
       x = '',
       y ='%',
       color = 'Legend',
       caption = 'Rate values have been index linked to 2022 inflation in order to compare like.' ) +
  #theme
  theme_report() +
  theme(panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank())

#patchwork output together
CPI_rate

```

#Who pays the most rates?
Residential rate payers as a group pay the highest amount of rates, \$80,892,140$ in total. 
However, the median rates for residential payers is \$4,003.52, compared to \$7,344.46 of commercial rate payers. 
Specialist rate payers pay the least at \$2,297.72, while Farming rate payers pay a median of \$3,403.05. 
Residential rate payers rates vary the least between the interquartile range.
So, while they vary less and pay less in general, because they are the largest category, they pay the most rates. Despite the commercial category paying higher per rating unit. With the highest rate payment being just over a million NZD. The discussion around who pays the most in rates typically refers to residential rate payers, because they pay the most in total due to making up the majority of the rate payment collection base. From here on, the focus is on residential rate payers (QV category is residential and lifestyle).

# Where are residential rates highest?
For the year 2026/27, within the residential rates category, the highest median rates are paid in the Otamatea suburb (\$5,213.6), but the least total rates (\$3,090,701). Otamatea has the highest valued houses, but the fewest houses (593), this is why. Gonville, on the other hand pays the most total rates (\$12,198,414), and lower medians rates ($3928,71). Gonville has the most houses (2916) of any suburb. 
So it isn't clear cut if your suburb causes higher rates. 

```{r graph 4 map, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}
#===== Map Graph function =====#
map_graph <- function(data, fill, title) {
data %>%
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(mapping=aes(fill = .data[[fill]]), col = 'white', linewidth = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_sf(xlim = w_bbox$x, ylim = w_bbox$y) + #need to change the rural district label to be visible
  #annotation
  geom_sf_label(mapping = aes(label = paste0(sa3_name, "\nn= ",as.character(count))), 
               size = 3) + 
  annotate("label", x = 1777000, y = 5584000,
           label = paste0("Rural\nn=", rural_count), 
           size = 3, fill = 'white') + #play with this to get the position right
  #Scale arguments
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = whanganui_palette(3),
                       limits = range(data[[fill]]),
                       name = paste0(title, "\n(Thousands)"),
                       labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1/1000)) +
  #Labels
  labs(title = "",
       subtitle = '',
       x = '',
       y = '') +
  #Theme
  theme_map() +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.0, 0.0),
        legend.justification = c(0, 0),
        legend.direction = "horizontal",
        text = element_text(family = "Inter"))
}
```

#A closer look by suburb.
Taking a closer look at the rates by suburb we can see that the highest residential rate is in Gonville! While Otamatea has a higher median and a lower spread of rates, Gonville is almost the excat same in total rates distribution as Castle Cliff, with the exception of a few major outliers that increase the sum of total rates paid. St John's Hill has a very wide distribution, despite being a high median rate suburb. Almost no suburb has rate below $,3000 (excluding outliers), with the exception of the very widely spread rural area. With the exception of Otamatea and Rural, the other suburbs are quite similar in median rates in that there is plenty of overlap visible in the box charts.

#Are rate payers all paying their 'fair share?'
So, who pays the most in residential rates? Proportionally, it is Otamatea rates payers. Their payments are larger than other rates payers not just in value, but also relative to all rates payers. Proportionally, the median is around 0.006 from 2023 onwards Even if they pay less as a combined group. St John's hill comes in second at 0.0059. Rural rate payers pay the least, at 0.0042. Note the quantile intervals. Central has the highest rateable units as outliers, while Otamatea has a few low valued outliers. There is overlap in each suburb with each other suburb. In general, the observation holds. Higher median rate paying suburbs pay more than their "fair" share. Obviously, "fair" here is a construct. Rates are not even, they are based off of QV value and SUIPs. 

```{r, fig.width=15, fig.height=8}
#==== Wrangling ====#
equal_prop <- Residential %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(prop = 100 / n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::crossing(suburb = unique(residential$suburb))

#prop data
prop_data <- Residential %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  mutate(prop = 100 * `total rates` / sum(`total rates`)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(year, suburb) %>%
  reframe(median_qi(prop, .width = c(.25, .50, .80, .95)))

#final data
graph_3_data <- prop_data %>%
  left_join(Suburb_rank %>% 
              select(suburb, rank), by = "suburb") %>%
  mutate(suburb_label = factor(
    paste0(suburb, ", rank = ", rank),
    levels = paste0(Suburb_rank$suburb, ", rank = ", Suburb_rank$rank)
  ))

#==== Graph ====#
proportion_graph <- graph_3_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = y)) +
  geom_lineribbon(aes(ymin = ymin, ymax = ymax),
                  color = "#DC0100", alpha = 0.5, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_line(data = equal_prop, aes(x = year, y = prop),
            col = "black", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ suburb_label, ncol = 5) +
  #scale arguments
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(x) x %% 100) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#C7E9F3", "#92B8D8", "#5C88BD","#2757A2"),
                    name = "Quantiles") +
  #labels
  labs(title = "Otamatea rate payers pay proportionally the most rates",
       subtitle = "The four more expensive suburbs pay proportionally more rates than cheaper ones.",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Proportion of rates paid per unit",
       caption = "Black dotted line is the proportion if every house paid the same share towards rates.") +
  #theme
  theme_report()
```

#area

Land area does not  equal land value. 
Do high QV values cluster together in such a way I can show it?
QV values are calculated based off of some external process. If one goes up, then others nearby do too. Therefore, there is no obvious pattern in the area or SUIP or location of a home. QV based rates are not 'fair' in this sense. They end up accumulating rate value increases to place that see more high value sales. 


#Graph 4 - rain clouds by SUIP

What about SUIPs? Each SUIP pays a fixed portion to rates. Are their enough multiple SUIPs to explain the difference in rates?
No. Very few units are not single SUIP. Rural looks to have only slightly more0 or 2 SUIP units than other suburbs, but this is marginal at best. Most units are single SUIP. SUIPS cannot explain this discrepency - i.e. we do not see more SUIPs in higher valued suburbs. Even though total rates do increase with more SUIPs, this increase is obscurred at the aggregate level by the sheer volume of single SUIP units. 

only 779 units have 3+ SUIPs



```{r, fig.height=8, fig.width=10}

median_SUIP <- graph_4_data %>% summarise(median(`total rates`)) %>% pull()
```

#QV clustering

So, if rate payers are not paying equally based on house area, and SUIPs do not alone account for the variance, 
and we see that more expensive house contribute proportionally more, the question is why?

Rates are determiend by QV valuations. QV is the land value plus the capital value plus the difference between land and capital value which is called the improvement value. Then a process called mass appraisal is applied which takes into account market information and area, consents, revaluations and so on. 

What this means is that the rates are determined not by something which is 'fair', but by market desirability of a home. The more it is wanted (higher sale value) the higher the rates. In effect, rate payers are paying the QV valuation portion of their rates (there are fixed costs too) based on how much other people want to buy their homes. A tax for not selling. Every time people improve their homes, the value of nearby homes increases because the desirability has gone up for the whole street.  
If it were the case that a raise in one home value attracted raises in other nearby homes then we would expect to see clustering of similar QV values in similar suburbs and streets. This is what we see in the below graph. 
Each dot represents a unit, each cluster a group of similar QV values (50% similar). A tight cluster shows similar QV values in the same street. That clusters are always of the same colour indicates that QV similarity has a spatial proximity element. otherwise we'd see mixed coloured blobs. The network is naturally seprated into suburbs because streets tend not to cross suburbs often. This shows a natural ordering in the QV values. Suburbs and streets. 

Basically, if more people would like to live in your house (higher demand) and you don't sell, you pay a premium. 



```{r QV network, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#===== Wrangling =====#
set.seed(21)

street_data <- Residential %>% 
  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  select(property_no, assessment_number, property_address, suburb, QV, year, `total rates`) %>%
  mutate(
      street = str_remove(property_address, "~WHANGANUI.*$"),
      street = str_remove(street, "^\\s*\\d+\\s*"),
      assess_num = str_remove(assessment_number, "[A-Z]+$") |> as.numeric()
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(street)) %>%
  group_by(suburb) %>%
  slice_sample(prop = 1000 / nrow(street_data)) %>%
  ungroup() 

# Build edges using assessment_no as the ID. It it a proxy for closeness that is easier to work with. I looked through the data and that is what I saw. Streets were alphabetically arranged, by street number within suburbs with the property number indicating closeness. 
street_edges <- street_data %>%
  select(property_address, suburb, street, QV, assess_num) %>%
  rename(from = QV, from_id = assess_num) %>%
  left_join(
    street_data %>%
      select(property_address, suburb, street, QV, assess_num) %>%
      rename(to = QV, to_id = assess_num),
    by = c("suburb", "street"),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) %>%
  filter(
    from_id != to_id,
    #set the number of neighbours used... assessment ids are proxy for neighbouring units, so larger mean more nieghbours, smaller value here means fewer. 
    abs(from_id - to_id) <= 1000000000, #10 digits is max
    from_id < to_id
  ) %>%
  #price of point of origin, to the nearby units, normalised so 1 = the same QV, and 0 = most different. 
  mutate(sim = 1 - abs(from - to) / max(from, to)) %>%
  #toggle similarity level. 
  filter(sim >= 0.5) %>%
  select(from_id, to_id, sim, suburb)

# Build graph — vertices are property_no (unique)
g <- graph_from_data_frame(
  street_edges %>% select(from_id, to_id, sim, suburb),
  vertices = street_data %>%
    distinct(assess_num, suburb) %>%
    set_names(c("name", "suburb")),
  directed = FALSE
)

#===== Plot =====#
ggraph(g, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(edge_width = sim), alpha = 0.6, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = factor(suburb)), size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.2, 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_color_manual(values = whanganui_palette(10)) +  
  labs(title = "Similar location, similar QV.",
       subtitle = "Rateable units cluster within suburb streets, not between suburbs.",
       colour = "Suburb",
       caption = "network made with representative sample of 997 units.") +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        plot.title = element_text(size = 20),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 15))
```


So, who pays the most and why?
Well, people in higher valued suburbs pay more rates proportionally than other rate payers. They do this not really because of anything other than the fact that people want to live in higher valued suburbs. The market taxes them for the privilege. 

=============================================================================

So who pays the most?
Commercial rate payers on a per unit basis, but residential payers as a group. 
Of the residential payers who pays the most?
Payers in Otamatea pay higher median rates. Payer in Gonville pay the most as a group. 
Otamatea rate payers pay the most proportionally compared to the whole, which is not just because they have more expensive houses.
SUIP makes you pay more, but few have SUIP >= 3. Most are SUIP 1. With the most of these in Gonville. Fewest in Otamatea. 

If you have a home in Otamatea, you will pay more than other people relative to their homes.

##dendograms
Try a dendro gram. Show the street clusters. 

```{r}
library(ggdendro)

# Aggregate to street level: median rate per street
street_rates <- street_data %>%
  group_by(suburb, street) %>%
  summarise(median_rate = median(`total rates`), n = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n >= 3)

# Hierarchical clustering on median rate
dend <- hclust(
  dist(street_rates$median_rate),
  method = "ward.D2"
)

# Plot
ggdendro::ggdendrogram(dend) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Street", y = "Distance",
       title = "Street-level rate clustering",
       subtitle = "Tight clusters = streets with similar median rates")
```

```{r}
library(factoextra)

fviz_dend(
  hclust(dist(street_rates$median_rate), method = "ward.D2"),
  k = n_distinct(street_rates$suburb),  # one cluster per suburb
  cex = 0.6,
  rect = TRUE,
  labels_rot = 90,
  main = "Street rate clustering"
) +
  scale_color_manual(values = whanganui_palette(11),
                     name = "Cluster")
```

```{r}
# Normalise rate, then add suburb as a categorical distance
library(vegan)

# Binary matrix: one row per street, columns = suburbs (1 if that suburb)
suburb_mat <- model.matrix(~ 0 + suburb, data = street_rates)

# Combine rate distance + suburb distance
d_rate   <- dist(street_rates$median_rate)
d_suburb <- vegan::vegdist(suburb_mat, method = "jaccard")

# Weighted combination (tune the weight)
d_combined <- 0.7 * d_rate + 0.3 * d_suburb

dend <- hclust(d_combined, method = "ward.D2")

fviz_dend(dend, k = n_distinct(street_rates$suburb),
          cex = 0.6, rect = TRUE, labels_rot = 90,
          main = "Street clustering (rate + suburb)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = whanganui_palette(11),
                     name = "Cluster")
```
